title: Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire
description: ByLaura Gozzi and Vitaly ShevchenkoChief analyst, BBC MonitoringFighting has resumed in Ukraine's Kherson after a six-day truce brought quiet to the f
body: ByLaura Gozzi and Vitaly ShevchenkoChief analyst, BBC MonitoringFighting has resumed in Ukraine's Kherson after a six-day truce brought quiet to the front-line region for the first time in years.The ceasefire - the longest since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - allowed hundreds of people trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky and its surroundings to be evacuated.On Monday morning, local authorities confirmed that strikes had resumed, saying Moscow had hit a medical facility in Kherson city centre. They also said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were injured when a Russian drone attacked the car they were travelling in.Ukraine also accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian ceasefire to strengthen their military positions, rotate units and deliver ammunition."The enemy used the humanitarian pause to set up their positions," said Ukraine's General Staff, adding they had recorded rotation of Russian units, expansion of anti-drone equipment on the roads, and delivery of ammunition.The Kremlin appeared to corroborate this when spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was "reasonable to assume that the Ukrainian army also used this period for the necessary regrouping"."It is a completely standard practice in such situations," he added.The ceasefire had been brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump. Both Kyiv and Moscow thanked her repeatedly, though no details of her involvement were shared.An unusual show of cooperation came from Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets. The pair oversaw the ceasefire, travelled into Oleshky and were filmed speaking to residents together. They publicly thanked each other for their work, often highlighting that no violations of the ceasefire had been observed.Both Lantratova and Lubinets called for the initiative to be repeated elsewhere, and Ukraine repeatedly said it would be prepared to observe similar ceasefires on a national level too.But many have questioned whether this will lead to more cooperation and further truces.In fact, the Kremlin swiftly dismissed the idea even as the ceasefire was under way, calling Oleshky "an isolated case" which would not affect the "settlement process" – a euphemism for the stalled peace talks. "There are no similar plans or initiatives," Peskov reiterated on Monday. And although last week the guns fell silent in Kherson region, elsewhere in Ukraine Russia's air strikes continued, killing scores of civilians and destroying crucial infrastructure.The decision to observe an unusually broad and comparatively lengthy ceasefire in and around Oleshky was therefore a notable exception.The ceasefire's observance appears, at least in part, to have been linked to Melania Trump's reported involvement. By violating the truce, Moscow would have risked undermining its own efforts to cultivate the crucial relationship with her husband, US President Donald Trump.Some commentators have argued that Trump himself would be interested in presenting the Oleshky ceasefire as a foreign policy achievement scored days before the US midterm elections on Tuesday."I totally get why our official representatives need to 'play along' with the US first lady on Oleshky," said Artyom Sheynin, a prominent figure on Russian state TV."I understand why it's so important to create a 'success story' ahead of the elections for the US president, whose wife 'achieved a ceasefire' in Oleshky."Kyiv, too, had its reasons to be fully compliant. Although relations with the US and its president are often fraught, Ukraine continues to rely heavily on US intelligence and US-made Patriot air defence missiles to counter Russian aerial attacks. Ahead of another tough winter of war, continued American support is essential to protect Ukrainian skies from Russia's assaults.But though the ceasefire may have been born out of political calculation rather than purely humanitarian compassion, it also resulted in hundreds of civilians escaping.There were emotional scenes when hundreds of Oleshky residents arrived in northern Ukraine on Saturday. Many were met by tearful relatives they had not seen in years. To the journalists waiting, the evacuees told of years of hunger and hardship in a destroyed town.The hundreds of residents who decided to stay behind will receive monthly humanitarian aid deliveries, Lantratova said, adding that decision too was the result of Melania Trump's mediation.Yet the troop rotations and resupply efforts show that neither side is expecting Oleshky to be a blueprint for lasting respite in the future.As Kherson came under fire again, Ukrainian drones hit several energy facilities across four Russian regions. In Samara, residents reported hearing explosions and seeing black plumes of smoke rising into the sky as an oil refinery was hit for the fifth time in a month. If the truce brought a rare moment of relief to Oleshky, it has done little to alter the wider trajectory of a war that grinds on for now.

schema.headline: Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire

title: Fake nuclear warning from hacked app sparks unease but not panic in Ukraine
description: Ukrainians have grown weary of the relentless alerts blaring from their phones and echoing through their streets, day and night, warning of Russian dr
body: Ukrainians have grown weary of the relentless alerts blaring from their phones and echoing through their streets, day and night, warning of Russian drones and missiles.On Sunday night, the system delivered something to make them sit up and take note – a succession of more extreme threats that quickly escalated to impending nuclear strikes, chemical attacks and combat on the streets.But many in the country did not take them seriously and doubted the veracity of the messages.Sofia Kochmar, 34, a mother-of-one living in the western city of Lviv, said she was initially concerned but quickly questioned the authenticity of the alerts."The first thing I saw was the word 'nuclear' and that made me pretty nervous and scared. So my first thought was that something nuclear was actually flying toward us.""But then the notification mentioned 'street fighting in Kyiv', and I thought, wait, no, that's impossible."The alerts included some messages written in Russian, and one included a link to a Telegram channel apparently owned by a hacker group.  Within 15 minutes, Ukraine's Air Force issued a statement saying the alert app had been compromised and clarifying there was no radiation threat. But it took more than an hour to issue "all clear" messages.Anastasiia Romanytska, a 29-year-old ballerina living in Kyiv, said she does not have the alert app installed but friends forwarded her the warnings."My first reaction was, 'Is this some kind of joke?' But then my body reacted as if I was under stress. My heart started racing, and my stomach tightened up.""Still, somehow I immediately realised that it wasn't something serious. Or maybe I just really wanted to believe that."There are a number of apps delivering phone notifications of air raid warnings, with maps showing areas under threat, all using the same data as the official government-backed app. Yevhen Baliutov, a cybersecurity expert at Kyiv School of Economics, told the BBC it was clear to him the Ukrainian alert system was hacked by Russians, saying many Ukrainians had clicked a link included with the alerts leading to a Russian Telegram channel, potentially exposing them to further disinformation, phishing attempts or data breaches."This is a war, so it's no surprise that Russia will try to hack, will try to send us fake news, will try to manipulate, and will use that for their propaganda."While both Russia and Ukraine are widely believed to carry out cyberattacks against one another, the informal language used in the hoax alerts on Sunday pointed to so-called hacktivist groups, which could be aligned to Moscow or Kyiv but are not formally directed by either government.Baliutov said it was also logical that Ukraine would have responded by launching a cyber-attack on the Russian emergency alert system. Both sides have similar capabilities in cyber warfare, he added.Kochmar said after the initial concern, Ukrainians quickly turned to joking about the incident."All our work group chats immediately blew up. Everyone started messaging each other, discussing what was happening. And what I found fascinating was how quickly we turned the whole thing into a joke."Although the impact of this incident had been limited, it illustrated the weakness of a crucial system, Baliutov said."It's very dangerous for Ukraine and for our people. When developing such applications, we need to consider security from the very beginning, without skipping essential security measures. When millions of people rely on a service, we cannot afford to take shortcuts with security."The authorities already faced the challenge of maintaining public alertness after four and a half years of war with ceaseless attack warnings sounding sometimes hourly. Now they must reassure people the systems in place to protect them are robust, trustworthy and should be followed.

schema.headline: Fake nuclear warning from hacked app sparks unease but not panic in Ukraine

title: Copilot in deadly Florida jet crash identified in reports as 20-year-old
description: Figure caption, Dashcam footage captures Florida private jet crashByNardine SaadUpdated 1 hour agoA 20-year-old copilot was among nine people killed w
body: Figure caption, Dashcam footage captures Florida private jet crashByNardine SaadUpdated 1 hour agoA 20-year-old copilot was among nine people killed when a small jet crashed and exploded in Florida on Sunday, according to US media.Nathalia Filgueiras, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, is reported to have been one of two crew members aboard the Learjet 60 from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas when it crashed near West Palm Beach.The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said it would investigate to what extent ice and turbulence may have contributed to the crash, and whether human error played a role.One man on the ground sustained a leg injury when the aircraft nosedived on to a street near Cresthaven, nine miles (14 km) from President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort.Images from the scene show a large fiery crater in the middle of a residential suburban street. The debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area, officials told a news conference on Monday, possible evidence that the plane broke up before it hit the ground.Figure caption, Officials describe how Learjet flight unfolded before deadly crashThe NTSB confirmed that after the jet took off from Austin, the crew transmitted to air traffic control that they were encountering ice and moderate turbulence."We are picking up precipitation, requesting to climb to 37,000 feet if able," the crew said.NTSB member Tom Chapman said that less than 30 seconds later, the plane began to descend and the crew issued a mayday call.The transmission then became "unintelligible", he said, adding that: "Sadly, all aboard were lost."Flight analysis indicates the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before crashing.In air traffic control audio, a crew member can be heard declaring an emergency, shouting "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".About 35 seconds after the initial mayday announcement, the last remark from the cockpit was "we're out of time".Figure caption, Three years before crash, young copilot spoke of earning pilot licenceFilgueiras's mother, Camila Corteleti, confirmed to US media that her daughter had died in the fireball.Corteleti told the New York Times: "She loved the freedom. It was completely different seeing the world from the top."In a 2023 interview with a local news affiliate of CBS News, Filgueiras spoke proudly of receiving her pilot's licence while still a senior in high school."I like being different than everyone," she said. "Some people think that it's weird that I can fly planes, but I can't drive a car, I mean I can but, a lot of people think it's funny."None of the other eight people on board has been identified.The NTSB said that ice and turbulence were factors in the crash.Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was on board at the time of the crash and if it can be recovered.The NTSB said determining the probable cause of the crash will be a "lengthy investigatory process".As part of the investigation, the NTSB is working with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), representatives from Learjet as well as meteorologists and air traffic control experts.Recovering the wreckage from the crater on the roadway will be a "daunting challenge", said Timothy Monville, an air safety investigator with the NTSB.He added that an individual who was in a vehicle near the crash site sustained a leg injury. Image source, Nathalia Filgueiras / ThreadsUnverified footage posted on social media shows what appears to be a dash-camera recording of the moment of the crash. "When you see that video, it's a jarring thing," Florida Governor Ron DeSantis told reporters at a news conference on Sunday. "It's like a missile coming down, and a massive explosion, debris going everywhere."Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy described the crash as a "horrific tragedy".The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said the crash happened on Military Trail, a six-lane road lined with businesses and restaurants. Thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time of the crash.Trump was at Mar-a-Lago on Sunday morning, and departed from an airport nearby on Air Force One about an hour before the crash.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The jet crashed on a six-lane road

schema.headline: Copilot in deadly Florida jet crash identified in reports as 20-year-old

title: Prosecutors hint at plans to retry Lindsay Clancy on murder charges
description: Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicideMassachusetts prosecutors have given their clearest indication yet
body: Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicideMassachusetts prosecutors have given their clearest indication yet that they plan to retry Lindsay Clancy for the murder of her three children in 2023.At a hearing on Monday, Judge William Sullivan scheduled a 16 November hearing where he plans to rule on a handful of motions that could determine how a retrial would proceed, including a request to dismiss the first-degree murder charges.Clancy faced a weekslong trial on those charges over the summer. It fell apart in early September after a 12-person jury failed to reach a verdict. If there is a retrial, Judge Sullivan said, it could happen as soon as March 2027.The prosecution did not say on Monday whether Clancy would face the same charges or amended charges in the event of a retrial. When the parties meet again later this month, they will hear the judge's rulings on the motions argued in court on Monday, and potentially will discuss dates for a retrial, Judge Sullivan said.Kevin Reddington, Clancy's attorney, pushed the judge for a spring trial."I am not going to have this woman sit incarcerated for the next year or two or three," he said. "I want a date and I want it this spring."But prosecutor Jennifer Sprague said she wants to hear Judge Sullivan's rulings on   Monday's arguments before the prosecution commits to a new date or specifics for a potential retrial.When the judge asked for more details on how prosecutors planned to proceed with a potential retrial, Sprague responded: "This would be a retrial - as to what that looks like will depend". But that appeared to frustrate Reddington. "Why do we not know if the next trial is going to be murder in the first degree or a lesser charge, why do they need to wait for the motions? I need to know logistically."Clancy was charged with three counts of first-degree-murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.Prosecutors could decide to bring lesser charges against Clancy in a retrial. For example, second-degree-murder charges, apply to unlawful killings committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning.Despite Sprague's statement in court, District Attorney Timothy Cruz has not yet   confirmed that Clancy will face a retrial and has not announced future plans for the case. Much of Monday's conversations in court focused on the one holdout juror, also known as Juror Doe, and the defence's investigation into him. Juror Doe disagreed with the other jurors, who appeared to want to find Clancy not guilty by way of insanity. The lack of agreement led to a hung jury and mistrial.In some of the most fiery moments of the three-hour hearing on Monday, Reddington requested a plethora of evidence including the holdout juror's phone and phone records. Heather O'Connor, the attorney who represents Juror Doe, said she was in court because Clancy's defence team has "combined several allegations" to try to argue that a mistrial should not have been declared, she said.That is among the motions Sullivan said he will rule on in a few weeks.Clancy does not deny killing her children, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors claim the killings were intentional.

schema.headline: Prosecutors hint at plans to retry Lindsay Clancy on murder charges

title: King's role is not policy making, says Palace in slavery apology row
description: The King's role as head of the Commonwealth is about "inspiring and convening, rather than policy making", says Buckingham Palace - distancing him fro
body: The King's role as head of the Commonwealth is about "inspiring and convening, rather than policy making", says Buckingham Palace - distancing him from rows over whether the UK should apologise and make reparations for its part in the Atlantic slave trade.The Palace statement clarifying the King's non-political role in the Commonwealth comes as the organisation's leaders gather for a summit in Antigua and Barbuda.The King is to deliver a speech on Tuesday which is expected to recognise the painful legacy of slavery. But his speech will reflect the position of the UK government. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham had suggested there could be some form of apology over slavery, but has ruled out financial reparations.The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations.On Saturday, the prime minister said that the UK "must face up to the past" over the "brutal and barbaric violation" of the slave trade, and that he was "open" to the possibility of a formal apology. But on Monday, his official spokesperson said that while Burnham had "expressed his sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering caused by the transatlantic slave trade", this was "distinct from a formal apology". Burnham thought it was "right that a formal apology is discussed properly with the countries and communities most affected", his spokesperson said. "An apology of this significance should be informed by the people and countries most affected," they added. Meanwhile Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK was "self-confident enough to have this conversation"."The dialogue we're setting up will consider whether and how a formal apology could help acknowledge the history, help heal the division and support stronger relationships for the future," Miliband said.Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has rejected "endless talk about apologies" as a "distraction" from solving the UK's current problems.Gaston Brown, Prime Minister of Antigua and Barbuda, the country which is hosting the Commonwealth gathering, says that the consequences of slavery "have not disappeared with the passage of time" and wants to discuss reparations.Whichever way the King's speech addresses the subject of slavery will be a political decision.On previous occasions, the King has used strong language, such as talking about his "greatest sorrow and regret" at the "abhorrent and unjustifiable acts of violence" of the colonial era on a visit to Kenya.And in Antigua he is expected to voice his "sincere sorrow", having spoken about the "great suffering of the past" in the Bahamas last week.

schema.headline: King's role is not policy making, says Palace in slavery apology row

title: US midterms campaign set to be most expensive ever recorded
description: The top 40 donors gave $2.4bn up until 14 October, according to the liberal-leaning think tank Brennan Center for Justice, external, which is a record
body: The top 40 donors gave $2.4bn up until 14 October, according to the liberal-leaning think tank Brennan Center for Justice, external, which is a record high for that point in a midterms cycle."Spending in the 2026 midterms is shattering records, with more of the money coming from the wealthiest donors and groups this election," says Michael Beckel, a US campaign finance expert.As well as individuals, organisations can also give to Pacs. For example, Geosor Corp and Fund for Policy Reform, both founded by the billionaire financier George Soros, have given a combined $102m to liberal groups.Aside from Soros, former New York City mayor and businessman Michael Bloomberg has been the biggest Democratic donor, giving more than $60m.Several billionaires including Jeff Yass, who runs one of the world's largest trading firms, and Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein, the owners of a US business supply company, have given over $100m this campaign to Republican causes, according to FEC filings.But Musk has given by far the most of any individual, donating almost half a billion dollars as of October.

schema.headline: US midterms campaign set to be most expensive ever recorded

title: Man caught in car with £14k of drugs as a lamb ate chips in the back seat avoids jail
description: Image source, Police ScotlandImage caption, Pablo the lamb was later returned to its ownerA man who was caught in a car with £14,000 of drugs, while a
body: Image source, Police ScotlandImage caption, Pablo the lamb was later returned to its ownerA man who was caught in a car with £14,000 of drugs, while a lamb ate from a bag of chips in the back seat, has avoided jail.John McNeil, 56, was a passenger in Lindsey Sangster's vehicle which was stopped by police on the M74 in Glasgow on 22 April 2023.Bags of heroin and cocaine were later recovered by a police dog underneath the front passenger seat of the Volkswagen Golf.When quizzed about the animal - called Pablo - a sergeant claimed Sangster's partner McNeil told him she was a "trainee shepherdess." The duo were found guilty in September of possession of cocaine and diamorphine with intent to supply.Image source, SpindriftImage caption, John McNeil told jurors in his evidence that he was experienced with animalsThe pair claimed they had tried to save the lamb - named after Colombian drug lord Pablo Escobar - from a "dangerous position" on the middle of the road.The court previously heard Pablo belonged to North Lanrigg Farm in Motherwell, which is owned by farmer Kirsty Mair.A joint minute of agreed evidence said Mair had not given them permission to have the lamb.Sgt Nick Twigg, 42, told jurors that he had reason to stop Sangster's car on the motorway, with Sangster, McNeil and another man in the vehicle.An initial search found a glass pipe in the driver's door pocket while others were seized from McNeil and the man.He said:  "I asked Sangster where it [the lamb] came from and McNeil said that she was a trainee shepherdess."Prosecutor Julianna Keenan asked the officer if there was evidence of this and he replied: "No, the lamb at the time was eating a bag of chips left on the back seat. There were no bottles."A police dog named Billy later found £4,640 of cocaine and £10,050 of heroin under the front passenger seat within two bags.The purity of the cocaine was stated to be no less than 76%.In a joint minute of agreed evidence, Keenan said: "Officers were of the opinion that the circumstances of this case indicate the supply of cocaine and heroin due to the amount recovered being excessive for personal use."Pablo was taken to a farm in Ayrshire where it was held for 48 to 72 hours before being returned to Mair.A charge of resetting the lamb was dropped by the Crown mid-trial as there was "no reported theft" at the time.McNeil told jurors in his evidence that he had experience with animals, having worked in the past with his father, who is a retired agricultural contractor.He stated they came across Pablo on the middle of the road on the way home to Ayrshire after a journey to Edinburgh for the other man to purchase a car.McNeil claimed that Pablo was "dehydrated" and appeared not have been fed for a couple of hours.He told the court that the plan was to "take him back to the owner" as Pablo had identity markings on his ears.'At the height of his addiction'McNeil denied any knowledge of the drugs in the car, as did Sangster.Jurors were told that Sangster was under the influence of drugs at the time when she was behind the wheel and pleaded guilty at separate proceedings.She was disqualified from driving for 18 months and ordered to do 100 hours of unpaid work.Bronwyn Moore, defending McNeil at the sentencing, said her client was now a team leader at a construction company and that he was  "at the height of his addiction" when arrested.McNeil, of Fairlie, North Ayrshire, was back in the dock to be sentenced while Sangster, of Kilbirnie, did not appear and a warrant was granted for her arrest.Sheriff Tony Kelly ordered McNeil to do 300 hours of unpaid work and tagged him for six months, meaning he must stay indoors between 20:00 and 05:00.The sheriff said he had been advised the risk of McNeil offending again was low.After the lamb was returned to Mair, she said he was in fine health and happy with "his new pet lamb pals".

schema.headline: Man caught in car with £14k of drugs as a lamb ate chips in the back seat avoids jail

title: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
description: Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and
body: Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely."The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack.In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked.Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK.In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost €100,000 (£83,500) worth of produce. The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop.Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open.A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked.Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected".In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit. A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network"."ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.One of the ICA branches located in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores. The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem.The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia.In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator.A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores.A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.Additional reporting by Shiona McCallumHave you been affected by the issues raised in this story? Click here or use the form below.

schema.headline: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack

title: Two boys arrested after Chandler's Ford Halloween party stabbings
description: Two teenage boys have been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after five teenagers were stabbed at a Halloween party.Officers said they were ca
body: Two teenage boys have been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after five teenagers were stabbed at a Halloween party.Officers said they were called shortly after 22:30 GMT on Saturday to Park Road in Chandler's Ford, Hampshire, where an "unknown group" had gained entry to the event.Police said two boys remain in hospital having suffered serious injuries, with one 17-year-old victim in a life-threatening condition. The others have been discharged from hospital.A 17-year-old and 16-year-old, both from Southampton, have been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder and remain in police custody.Two witnesses told the BBC a fight started after a group came in over a garden fence, although they said the motive for the stabbings was unclear.One of the teenagers said: "I was [standing] in the hallway near the exit and I saw someone I know pull up their shirt and say 'I've been stabbed'."And then I later saw him lying outside the front of the house with someone compressing his wound."Police cordoned off parts of Park Road and the adjoining Valley Road.Det Ch Insp Elizabeth Pirie said: "Whilst the two arrests are a significant development in our investigation, which has moved at pace since the incident was first reported to us, we still urge our communities to contact us with any information, no matter how small it may seem."She added: "If you were at the party and have not spoken with officers yet, or you have any CCTV, mobile phone, dash cam or doorbell camera footage covering Park Road and the surrounding area, then please get in touch."

schema.headline: Two boys arrested after Chandler's Ford Halloween party stabbings

title: Democrats have high hopes for midterms - but are the polls right?
description: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesByNorth America correspondentThe Democratic Party has high expectations as it heads into these pivotal US midt
body: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesByNorth America correspondentThe Democratic Party has high expectations as it heads into these pivotal US midterm elections.A historically unpopular Republican president, an American public unhappy with the rising costs of food and bills, and months of favourable polls point to a good night for them on Tuesday.Democratic candidates lead in well over the 218 seats needed to flip control of the lower chamber of Congress, the House of Representatives, the polls suggest. And they are tied or narrowly ahead in the key Senate races.A recent New York Times poll had the Senate race in South Carolina, a state Donald Trump won by 18 percentage points in 2024, as a tie. Recent CNN surveys put the Democrats ahead in Texas, Kansas and Maine.But are the polls accurate?Recent US political history is littered with examples where public opinion polls, even ones just days before an election, were off the mark. Trump outperformed predictions on his way to White House victories in 2016 and 2024. His narrow defeat in 2020 came after most surveys indicated a more comfortable win for Democrat Joe Biden.Earlier this year, polls suggested Democrat Abdul El-Sayed was poised for a double-digit win in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary. Instead it was 1%. In Wisconsin's Democratic primary for governor, the candidate that had a polling lead that approached 20 points lost by a fraction of a percent.According to Clifford Young, president of Ipsos Public Affairs, which conducts political and market research surveys, polling has become difficult in recent years because it's harder to reach Americans as they abandon their land lines and screen their calls. And many of those who pollsters do contact have become less willing to participate."Conservatives, especially those on the far right, are much more anti-establishment by nature," Young says. "And they don't participate in anything. They hate the system. That's the challenge."If Republican voters are being undercounted in a systematic way, and polling companies don't take that into consideration when constructing their voting models, it could skew their data towards the Democrats.That's one of the reasons why it has become trickier for pollsters to predict what the electorate will look like.Figure caption, What's at stake for Trump in the US midterms?In recent years, midterm general election polls have proven to be more accurate, in part because Trump - and his unique ability to draw disaffected Americans to the polls - was not on the ballot.In 2022, they suggested Democrats would defy conventional expectations and avoid an electoral wipe-out despite Biden's low approval numbers.While the party lost control of the House of Representatives, the margins were slim and Democrats maintained control of the US Senate.While this year's primary results did provide bigger surprises, Young says that nominating contests have historically been volatile, with voters more likely to make up their minds at the last minute. It shouldn't be seen as an indication that the current crop of general election polls are off the mark.It's common for the party of the president to have a bad night in the midterms.One of the most notable examples in recent years came in 2010 when Republicans flipped more than 60 House seats and made gains in the Senate. It came off the back of an economy struggling to recover from the financial crash and conservative fears over President Barack Obama's healthcare reforms. A defeat had been predicted by the polls but not quite on that scale.The roles are reversed this time, with the Democrats in opposition and the economy on the minds of voters. But there are a number of reasons why Democrats may not have as good a night as history might suggest or as some might expect, given Trump's low approval rating.Firstly, much of the territory in play in this election Trump conquered with ease in the presidential election just two years ago. It's like a home game for Republicans.Then there have been changes to House election boundaries over the years that have meant fewer seats switch between parties.Thirdly, there are fewer swing voters due to the deeper polarisation of the country. Some experts describe the electorate as calcified.There's also the cash advantage Republicans have enjoyed which has given them hundreds of millions of dollars to spend on attack ads in the final weeks.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Obama gives a press conference the day after the heavy 2010 midterms defeatPolling models try to capture shifting fundamentals. And a well-designed poll is built to anticipate issues that may make it less than reliable.Individual polls do have a built-in margin of error – a statistical level of uncertainty based on the sampling size compared to the population as a whole. Taken as an aggregate, polling averages and not individual surveys can provide a more accurate prediction.At the moment, even the kind of polling lean we saw in recent presidential elections would suggest Democrats are likely to have a good night on 3 November. And polling inaccuracies can go both ways. In last year's state and special elections, Democrats outperformed most surveys as it was their voters who turned out in unexpectedly larger numbers.The sight of Trump holding rallies in the final days of the campaign in states he won comfortably in 2024 will have lifted Democrats' hopes that Republican internal polling has conservative candidates in trouble.Figure caption, Voter voices: What issues matter most to Americans?There's always the chance that voters change their minds right up until election day, however.Sometimes there are late shifts that can alter the dynamics of a race. Sometimes undecided voters, which still account for a key segment of the electorate in many of these races, all break the same way.In polling, there will always be some level of uncertainty – and managing that is the art that goes along with the science."I think we're doing a better job," says Young. "But part of the problem we always have is not just with the pollsters. Part of it is that we're dealing with humans. Humans are not easy."Do you have questions about the US midterms? Click here or use the form below.Get in touchWhat questions do you have?Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Democrats have high hopes for midterms - but are the polls right?

title: If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?
description: Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabiliti
body: Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabilities of internet-connected hardware from industrial machinery to humble domestic appliances.Smart devices which are connected to the internet can include fridges, central heating, and even washing machines.And while that makes them easier to control remotely, in theory, any device which goes online can potentially be exploited by malicious actors.However, that doesn't mean hackers can easily take control of it, and big brands generally go to great lengths to make sure their tech is secure.Exploits have been found before in some devices. In 2015, researchers demonstrated how a vulnerability in a Samsung smart fridge could allow them to intercept internet traffic.But there's no evidence domestic appliances are being targeted in the cyber-attacks which targeted supermarkets in November.Ciaran Martin, former chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says manufacturers needed to do more to make connected devices secure."There's a lot more that we need to demand of big tech to give us safer devices and products in the first place," he said.He advised consumers to keep devices updated and enable multi-factor authentication wherever possible."I know it's a pain, but it only takes a few seconds," he said.Since April 2024, UK law has required manufacturers of certain consumer smart devices to meet minimum cyber security standards, including requirements around passwords and security updates.The NCSC said it was working with international partners and industry to understand the supermarket incidents, but it was unaware of any impact on the UK.However, researchers from UK Cyber Defence have identified more than 800 refrigeration and building-control interfaces associated with British retailers that can be accessed over the public internet.That doesn't necessarily mean they can be hacked, but it could leave them exposed to attackers exploiting weak passwords or software vulnerabilities.The government has already held talks with senior food retailers about cyber resilience, following earlier attacks on supermarkets.Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, has said cyber incidents are a major concern for retailers, with businesses working alongside the NCSC to share intelligence and strengthen their defences.It would not be the first time that hacks have raised concern about impact on food supply.When UK supermarkets M&S and the Co-op were targeted by ransomware hackers in May 2025, the retailers struggled to stock some shop shelves with fresh deliveries.Customers across the UK complained of empty shelves in the days following the attack.Tom Hegel, a researcher at cyber-security firm SentinelOne, said retailers must be clearer about responsibility."The question retailers need to answer is who owns the security of that equipment, not just who repairs it," he said.He said internet connectivity can make everyday technology more convenient, but security needed to keep pace."Once an attacker can operate those controls, legitimate functions such as defrosting become tools for disruption," he said."Changing a setting can destroy physical stock, not just interrupt a computer system."Could cars, power plants and water supplies be vulnerable?Outside of the home, connected tech is used to remotely manage industrial machinery and vehicles.Cyber security expert Ken Munro pointed to a 2015 demonstration in which researchers remotely hacked a Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, prompting improvements in vehicle security."Fortunately, the vehicle industry woke up to this and fixed the problem," he said.  Mobile connections are also widely used to monitor equipment in power plants and water networks, allowing engineers to manage systems remotely.Munro said UK utilities were generally good at securing these connections, but standards varied around the world.His biggest concern was smaller, poorly funded utility companies which may still be relying on older, vulnerable equipment.Without proper protections, "any factory or equipment" connected to the internet - ranging from carmakers to electricity or transport infrastructure - could face similar risks, said Olivier Daloy, a cybersecurity expert at Zscaler.

schema.headline: If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?

title: Mahmood scraps settlement plans for migrant care workers
description: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has scrapped plans to make foreign care workers already in the UK wait 15 years to qualify for permanent settlement.Mah
body: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has scrapped plans to make foreign care workers already in the UK wait 15 years to qualify for permanent settlement.Mahmood had proposed doubling the wait for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) from five years to 10 for most migrants, with some facing a 15-year wait.But following a backlash from several Labour MPs, Mahmood revised the policy and care workers who earn at least £25,000 a year and arrived in the UK before May 2025 would continue to qualify after five years.The Conservatives said Mahmood's "U-turn" would cost taxpayers billions of pounds.ILR, also known as settlement, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible. They can also use it to apply for British citizenship.Last November, Mahmood announced plans to delay settlements in response to concerns over the number of people approaching eligibility, in the wake of record post-Brexit net migration figures under the previous Conservative government.The Home Office has said its figures show net migration - the difference between those entering and leaving the country - added 2.6m people to the UK population between 2021 and 2024.The department estimates that between 2026 and 2030 between 1.3m and 2.2m people will settle in the UK, adding its central estimate has increased to 1.9m.The home secretary faced criticism for proposing to apply the changes to migrant workers already in the UK, with Housing Secretary Angela Rayner previously saying this would "change the goalposts".Several Labour MPs also described the retrospective approach as "un-British" and  warned it could worsen the UK's skills shortage, particularly in the care sector.Making a statement to the House of Commons, Mahmood said settlement "should not be automatic, it should be earned".She said those who do not come under the various exceptions would be on a 10-year path to settlement status. This will still affect many people who came to the UK expecting to qualify after five years.One of those affected is Ashfak Juned, a Bangladeshi chef working in Birmingham, who told the BBC he was  "crying" when he heard the new rules, which will double his wait for settled status.The changes will move those earning less than £50,000 a year onto a 10-year path to settlement status, unless they are exempt, so he will have to wait until 2033, five more years than expected, before he can qualify for permanent settlement.Mahmood also told MPs the government would provide a five-year path to settlement for care workers who "answered our call when we needed them" following the Covid-19 pandemic.Mahmood said: "Those who earn £25,000 a year working in the social care sector, which was the condition of their visa, will therefore be able to settle on their existing five-year path."She added those care workers who did not meet the conditions of their visa will be offered "a second chance to make the contribution that they came to this country to make". They can apply for another five-year visa and seek settlement after this.The home secretary confirmed a number of groups would see their settlement path remain as it is today - including Hong Kong British nationals overseas, armed forces members, people with a British connection and those on legacy routes including the Windrush scheme.MPs were also told: higher earners on salaries of more than £50,000 and those who have contributed in healthcare and education, such as doctors and teachers, will be able to qualify for settlement after five yearsthe highest rate taxpayers earning more than £125,000 will be able to apply after three yearsrefugees who arrived in the UK after crossing the Channel by small boat or another illegal route will have to wait 20 years if they work or study, and 30 years if they do not.Mahmood said: "Our changes ensure those who are net contributors are encouraged to come to this country and stay here."She added: "As a result, the Department for Work and Pensions estimates that our reforms will reduce the benefits bill by billions of pounds."The original version of the plans announced by Mahmood last year would have delayed 799,000 people from gaining permanent residency.Under the updated plans announced on Monday, that number will now drop to 517,000.The Refugee Council's Imran Hussain condemned the plans for those who had travelled to the UK illegally or by small boat and do not work or study to wait 30 years for indefinite leave to remain as "unfair and unworkable".He said the plans would "condemn refugees to decades of deep insecurity" and "create another bureaucratic nightmare" for the Home Office."There is no evidence to suggest that harming refugee integration will act as a disincentive to refugees fleeing the Taliban or brutal conflicts like Sudan," he said."The fairest reforms would be making fast and good quality asylum decisions, with those refugees granted protection being helped to rebuild their lives and to contribute, and those with no right to remain helped to leave with dignity."For the Conservatives, shadow home secretary Chris Philp said: "It took a year for the home secretary to build her reputation as tough on immigration."But what took a year to build, she has just dismantled in 12 short minutes."Philp said opposition from fellow ministers and the "Labour open borders left" had resulted in the changes, adding Mahmood was "no longer running the government's immigration policy".He highlighted figures from March in which Home Office calculations suggested 196,000 care workers and their adult dependants could settle between 2026 and 2030, at an estimated lifetime cost of £9.5bn to taxpayers.Philp said this was the "cost of today's U-turn".But Father of the House Sir Edward Leigh, the longest-serving male MP in the Commons, criticised his Conservative colleague for overseeing the so-called Boriswave after Brexit, where net migration peaked at nearly one million in 2023."Some of us don't have amnesia," he said. "Many of us in that period in 2023 were putting this to our then government and anybody who was serving as a Home Office minister in that period should wear sackcloth and ashes, and frankly we will never move on until we accept that."Philp was a Home Office minister from 2022 to 2024, a period when the government relaxed immigration rules to introduce a post-Brexit Australian-style points-based system and welcomed an influx of non-EU migrants.Labour MP Diane Abbott welcomed the exemption for care workers from the new ILR arrangements, adding: "But for the rest of the workforce the retrospective nature of these new arrangements still seems to be unfair."Because you can come in legally, you can work legally but then have your residency rights turned upside down."Mahmood said she did not agree with Abbott's characterisation, adding every government needs to be able to make changes to immigration rules to respond to circumstances.Liberal Democrat home affairs spokesman Max Wilkinson said the government's reforms are "unravelling".He added: "Viewing immigration simply as a matter of raw numbers and images of small boat arrivals is degrading this nation's ability to have the informed national discussion that we need."Reform UK leader Nigel Farage branded the decision "the beginning of the capitulation" and said it would "cost this country a vast amount of money".Green Party MP Siân Berry said Mahmood had provided a "new obstacle course of hoops and barriers" for migrants living in the UK.On Monday, the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) think tank said that skilled workers and their dependants due to settle in the UK under current rules are expected to make a net lifetime contribution of around £115bn through the taxes they pay.

schema.headline: Mahmood scraps settlement plans for migrant care workers

title: Legal challenge to Australia's social media ban to start in High Court
description: Two days of hearings on a challenge to Australia's landmark social media ban for children will begin at the country's highest court on Tuesday.In a ma
body: Two days of hearings on a challenge to Australia's landmark social media ban for children will begin at the country's highest court on Tuesday.In a major test of the world-leading policy, a digital rights group will argue that the ban for under-16s robs children of their right to free communication. A separate challenge launched by platform Reddit will be jointly heard.Introduced last December, the ban is a key part of sweeping changes the Australian government has spearheaded in recent years on online safety.Supporters say the ban protects children from harmful content but critics say it is too blunt an instrument and efforts should focus on improving online safety.The constitutional challenge in Australia's High Court was filed by the Digital Freedom Project a few weeks before the ban started on 10 December last year. The group is lead by New South Wales parliamentarian John Ruddick.Two teens who originally spearheaded the case, Noah Jones and Macy Neyland, have since withdrawn as plaintiffs though Jones is still expected to attend Tuesday's hearing.Speaking about the legal challenge last November, Jones told the BBC that there were bad things online but a blanket ban for under-16s was not the right answer. "We shouldn't be using the resources and money of these social media platforms to try to avoid fines from our government," he said."They should be using this money and resources to try to get rid of the predators and harmful content out there."Reddit also launched a High Court challenge to the ban, arguing the policy has serious implications for privacy and political rights.Communications Minister Anika Wells last year said the government would not be "intimidated by legal threats." "We will not be intimidated by big tech. On behalf of Australian parents, we will stand firm," she said last November. Under the ban, ten platforms - Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, Snapchat, X, Kick, Threads and Twitch - must take "reasonable steps" to ensure no one under 16 years old can access its site.Platforms risk fines of up to A$99m (US$70m, £52m) for serious or repeated breaches, but since the ban started, no company has been fined.

schema.headline: Legal challenge to Australia's social media ban to start in High Court

title: What are the planned changes to immigration rules?
description: A partner who arrives with someone who then applies for ILR will be able to settle at the same time, as long as they meet the relevant requirements.Ho
body: A partner who arrives with someone who then applies for ILR will be able to settle at the same time, as long as they meet the relevant requirements.However, a partner who joins later will need to complete the same qualifying residence period before they are eligible for settlement.Eligible couples will be able to combine their earnings to meet the minimum income  requirement.The household income threshold will be £25,142 – twice the individual minimum income requirement.Children under 18 will continue to be able to settle with their parents.They will be exempt from the income, government debt, English language and Life in the UK test requirements, but will remain subject to the relevant suitability and criminality requirements.Young adults aged 18 to 24, who remain dependant on their family, will also continue to be able to settle alongside them.They will be expected to meet all the adult mandatory requirements but not the individual income requirement.Someone who is aged 25 or over when their family becomes eligible for settlement will be expected to qualify independently.Eligible partners, parents and children of British citizens will continue to qualify for settlement after five years.

schema.headline: What are the planned changes to immigration rules?

title: Russian bombing kills 26 people at humanitarian aid centre in Ukraine, Kyiv says
description: Figure caption, Video shows smoke rising from Komyshuvakha blast craterByJaroslav LukivUpdated 1 minute agoAt least 26 people were killed after Russia
body: Figure caption, Video shows smoke rising from Komyshuvakha blast craterByJaroslav LukivUpdated 1 minute agoAt least 26 people were killed after Russian bombs hit an aid distribution centre, in an attack that Ukraine's leader has called "utterly horrific".Five people were injured and 27 initially reported missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit the village of Komyshuvakha in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.President Volodymyr Zelensky said that after the first strike on the local school "used for humanitarian needs", there was a second attack on the place where people were sheltering. He posted a video showing a huge crater left after Monday's attack, and rescuer teams searching through the rubble.The Russian military has not publicly commented.Image source, DSNS / ZaporizhzhiaImage caption, There are fears that the death toll will rise further as a number of people are still under the rubbleZelensky initially put the death toll at 18, but Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS later said 24 people, including two rescuers and four police officers, were confirmed to have been killed. In his video address late on Monday, Zelensky said 26 people were now known to have died.He earlier said that "the Russians could not have been unaware that the local residents who remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid there every week" on Monday."This is yet another proof that Russia does not want any de-escalation."He said that after a recent successful joint Russian-Ukrainian operation to evacuate civilians from the Russia-occupied southern city of Oleshky during a temporary ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, "there was a moment when the next steps could show that peace is possible"."With such killings, Russia is sending the exact opposite signal - Russia is counting on further killings," Zelensky said.Image source, National police of UkraineImage caption, The Russian strikes left a huge crater where Ukrainian officials say people were shelteringMeanwhile, Semikin described the Russian attack as a "terrible tragedy" for the village, confirming that "people are still under the rubble". He said rescue teams were working at the scene, but they had been forced to halt their operation a number of times because of Russian drone attacks in the area.A day of mourning has been declared for Tuesday across the entire Zaporizhzhia region.Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Teams from Ukraine, Russia and the US are due to resume peace talks in the next few days after negotiations were suspended in February, with Moscow stepping up attacks as Kyiv virtually ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.However, no major breakthrough is expected at the talks that are likely to be held in Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates.

schema.headline: Russian bombing kills 26 people at humanitarian aid centre in Ukraine, Kyiv says
